Figure 1:Leaderboard of theCollaborative Intelligence Benchmark. Overall score of every model, the mean over the
8 dimensions of the test score on the tasks the model solves alone. Error bars give the 95% bootstrap
interval.

Figure 2:TheCollaborative Intelligence Benchmarkat a glance. (1) Each task starts from a real record or a benchmark item. (2) Every task runs
alone, in a team where nothing goes wrong, and in the test, which runs three times. (3) A task counts toward the score only if the model solves it alone.

header: 3How Well Do Models Work as Teammates?

8 dimensions.Solved alone, tasks the model passes alone, the only ones scored.Baseline, score

Figure 3:Where each model breaks. Test score of every model at its default setting on each dimension, with the
dimensions ordered from the hardest to the easiest.Table5gives the intervals and the high-effort runs.

Figure 4:The cost of a score. Score against the API cost of each row’s whole evaluation, at list prices (log scale).
A ring marks high reasoning effort. The dashed line is the Pareto frontier, which joins the rows that no cheaper row
beats (bold labels).

Figure 5:Frontier models fail most often by taking a worse deal in a conflict, and DeepSeek V4 Pro most often by
missing the problem. Each bar is the share of test runs that fail in one mode (SectionG.3).

Figure 6:In five dimensions most failures come after the model saw the problem (a), and stronger models more often
fail this way (b).

header: 5How Do AI Agents Compare with People as Teammates?

images.caption:
Figure 7:Comparison with human results from the source studies. Each group names what the team does and the source
study. The models are scored as that study scored the people, but the instructions, incentives and settings are not
fully matched (SectionG.1).

Figure 9:Three checks of the score. In the first two, each point is one row ofTable5, scored in two ways. In
the third, each point is a pair of rows, compared on the tasks that both solve alone. The higher-ranked row wins in 271
of 276 pairs.

Figure 10:People check the judges on 40 messages. How often a person chooses the judges’ final label, and how
often the referee and the second rater choose the same label, on the same messages. The number of messages is in
brackets.

Figure 11:A smaller subset keeps the ranking. (a) Kendall’sτ\taubetween the
score on a random subset of public tasks (the same number from each dimension) and the full score, over the
24 rows. The star is the Lite subset, evaluated on rows that were not used to choose it. (b) Score on the
Lite subset against the full score.

Figure 12:Real-world records against benchmark-built tasks. (a) Each row’s score on the tasks built from
real-world records against its score on the tasks adapted from benchmarks and datasets, in the 7
dimensions that have both. (b) Mean test value by source family over the models at the default setting (bars, with the
value) and over the frontier models (diamonds). Teal bars are real-world records and slate bars are benchmarks and datasets (Table1).

Table 5:Test score by dimension for every result card (%), with half the 95% bootstrap interval in grey. The
rows include the runs at high reasoning effort (high).openmarks an open-weight model.

Figure 13:Teamwork profiles of the 18 models at the default setting, ranked by overall score (below each
name). Each radar gives the model’s test score on each dimension, against the mean of all 18 models (grey).
Models with similar overall scores can have very different profiles.

Figure 14:Where the score is lost. (a) For each model at the default setting, the tasks it solves alone, split into
those it also passes in the test, those it fails only in the test, and those it already fails in a calm team. Each
dimension counts equally. (b) The same split for each dimension, as the mean over the models. Taking over is not shown,
because its baseline is the original task and not a calm team.

Figure 15:Score by release date. Each model is at its best reasoning setting and is dated by the first day developers
could call the version we evaluated through a public API. The date axis is broken between 2025 and 2026. The grey dashed
line joins the models that beat every model released before them (bold labels), and the orange dashed line does the
same for open-weight models. Up to Kimi K3, every model that sets a new best is open-weight, so the two lines
coincide there. We test only current models, so the line shows when these models came out, not the history of the
field.

Table 6:Default against high reasoning effort. The overall score at each setting, the API cost of the evaluation at
high effort as a multiple of its cost at the default setting (Section3.3), and the tasks (solved alone at both
settings) whose test value rises or falls at high effort.ppis from a two-sided sign test.

Figure 18:Teamwork and general capability. (a) Score of each model at the default setting against the Artificial
Analysis Intelligence Index[69]. The dashed line is the least-squares fit, and each
label gives the distance from it in points. (b) Correlation of each dimension’s test score with the same index, over
the 17 models.

Figure 19:Handling conflict goes against the rest of teamwork.a, Pearson correlation between the
dimension scores of the 18 models at their default setting.b, How each model’s test runs with the
pushy teammate end. The best deal scores 1 point, holding firm without it 0.5 and giving in 0. Models are in order of
overall score.c, Share of these runs in which the model asks about the teammate’s needs, or gives in, against the
model’s mean score on the other seven dimensions. Lines are least-squares fits.

Table 8:How the conflict tests end, and the joint points of the deals. Conflict is the conflict score (best deal 1,
holding firm without it 0.5, giving in 0). No deal counts the runs that end without a deal, with either outcome. Joint
points are the points of the final deal for the whole team, as a share of the best joint points of the task, over
the runs that end with a deal. Models are in order of overall score.
